question: Generate a research proposal on low-resource speech recognition.
answer_a:
Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

**1. Title**
Cross-Lingual Phonetic Distillation (CLPD): Leveraging Shared Phonemic Embeddings for Ultra-Low-Resource ASR

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current state-of-the-art Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems rely on thousands of hours of labeled data. For the vast majority of the world’s 7,000+ languages, labeled data is either non-existent or limited to fewer than 10 hours. While self-supervised learning (SSL) models like wav2vec 2.0 or HuBERT provide a strong foundation, fine-tuning them on ultra-low-resource data often leads to overfitting or poor generalization. There is a need for a mechanism that explicitly transfers linguistic knowledge from high-resource "bridge" languages to low-resource target languages by exploiting universal phonetic similarities.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
By distilling the intermediate representations of a high-resource "teacher" model (trained on a linguistically related language) into a low-resource "student" model using a shared International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) bottleneck, we can achieve a lower Word Error Rate (WER) than standard cross-lingual fine-tuning. The hypothesis rests on the idea that phonetic features are more transferable across languages than graphemic features.

**4. Method**
*   **Stage 1: Teacher Training:** Train a wav2vec 2.0 base model on a high-resource "bridge" language (e.g., Spanish) to perform ASR, but modify the output layer to predict IPA phonemes instead of standard characters.
*   **Stage 2: Shared Embedding Space:** Map the target low-resource language’s phoneme set to the IPA space.
*   **Stage 3: Phonetic Distillation:** Fine-tune the student model on the low-resource target data (e.g., 1–5 hours). The loss function is a weighted combination of:
    1.  **CTC Loss:** Standard Connectionist Temporal Classification loss on the target language labels.
    2.  **Distillation Loss:** A Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the student’s transformer layer activations and the teacher’s activations, specifically when processing the same acoustic segments, focused on the phonetic feature extraction layers.
*   **Stage 4: Decoding:** Use a constrained beam search decoder that maps IPA outputs back to target language graphemes using a simple pronunciation lexicon.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **High-Resource (Teacher):** Common Voice (Spanish or French, ~500+ hours).
*   **Low-Resource (Student):** Common Voice "Low-Resource" subsets (e.g., Abkhaz, Guarani, or Wolof) limited to 1-hour and 5-hour training splits.
*   **Validation:** Standard development sets provided by Common Voice for each target language.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Word Error Rate (WER):** Primary metric for final transcription accuracy.
*   **Phoneme Error Rate (PER):** To evaluate the effectiveness of the phonetic transfer before the graphemic mapping.
*   **Real-Time Factor (RTF):** To ensure the distillation process does not result in an overly complex model for inference.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Baseline A (Monolingual SSL):** wav2vec 2.0 Base fine-tuned only on the target low-resource data.
*   **Baseline B (Multilingual SSL):** XLSR-53 (Cross-lingual Speech Representations) fine-tuned on the target data without specific distillation.
*   **Baseline C (Standard Transfer):** A model pre-trained on the high-resource language and directly fine-tuned on the target language (standard weight initialization transfer).

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Distillation:** Fine-tune using only the IPA bottleneck without the teacher-student MSE loss.
*   **Random Bridge:** Use a linguistically unrelated teacher (e.g., using an English teacher for a Mandarin-adjacent target) to measure the impact of linguistic distance.
*   **Layer-wise Distillation:** Apply distillation only to the CNN encoder versus only to the Transformer blocks.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Phonetic Mismatch:** If the bridge language lacks specific phonemes present in the target language (e.g., clicks or specific tones), the teacher may provide "noisy" or misleading guidance.

**1. Title**
Cross-Lingual Phonetic Distillation (CLPD): Leveraging Shared Phonemic Embeddings for Ultra-Low-Resource ASR

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current state-of-the-art Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems rely on thousands of hours of labeled data. For the vast majority of the world’s 7,000+ languages, labeled data is either non-existent or limited to fewer than 10 hours. While self-supervised learning (SSL) models like wav2vec 2.0 or HuBERT provide a strong foundation, fine-tuning them on ultra-low-resource data often leads to overfitting or poor generalization. There is a need for a mechanism that explicitly transfers linguistic knowledge from high-resource "bridge" languages to low-resource target languages by exploiting universal phonetic similarities.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
By distilling the intermediate representations of a high-resource "teacher" model (trained on a linguistically related language) into a low-resource "student" model using a shared International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) bottleneck, we can achieve a lower Word Error Rate (WER) than standard cross-lingual fine-tuning. The hypothesis rests on the idea that phonetic features are more transferable across languages than graphemic features.

**4. Method**
*   **Stage 1: Teacher Training:** Train a wav2vec 2.0 base model on a high-resource "bridge" language (e.g., Spanish) to perform ASR, but modify the output layer to predict IPA phonemes instead of standard characters.
*   **Stage 2: Shared Embedding Space:** Map the target low-resource language’s phoneme set to the IPA space.
*   **Stage 3: Phonetic Distillation:** Fine-tune the student model on the low-resource target data (e.g., 1–5 hours). The loss function is a weighted combination of:
    1.  **CTC Loss:** Standard Connectionist Temporal Classification loss on the target language labels.
    2.  **Distillation Loss:** A Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the student’s transformer layer activations and the teacher’s activations, specifically when processing the same acoustic segments, focused on the phonetic feature extraction layers.
*   **Stage 4: Decoding:** Use a constrained beam search decoder that maps IPA outputs back to target language graphemes using a simple pronunciation lexicon.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **High-Resource (Teacher):** Common Voice (Spanish or French, ~500+ hours).
*   **Low-Resource (Student):** Common Voice "Low-Resource" subsets (e.g., Abkhaz, Guarani, or Wolof) limited to 1-hour and 5-hour training splits.
*   **Validation:** Standard development sets provided by Common Voice for each target language.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Word Error Rate (WER):** Primary metric for final transcription accuracy.
*   **Phoneme Error Rate (PER):** To evaluate the effectiveness of the phonetic transfer before the graphemic mapping.
*   **Real-Time Factor (RTF):** To ensure the distillation process does not result in an overly complex model for inference.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Baseline A (Monolingual SSL):** wav2vec 2.0 Base fine-tuned only on the target low-resource data.
*   **Baseline B (Multilingual SSL):** XLSR-53 (Cross-lingual Speech Representations) fine-tuned on the target data without specific distillation.
*   **Baseline C (Standard Transfer):** A model pre-trained on the high-resource language and directly fine-tuned on the target language (standard weight initialization transfer).

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Distillation:** Fine-tune using only the IPA bottleneck without the teacher-student MSE loss.
*   **Random Bridge:** Use a linguistically unrelated teacher (e.g., using an English teacher for a Mandarin-adjacent target) to measure the impact of linguistic distance.
*   **Layer-wise Distillation:** Apply distillation only to the CNN encoder versus only to the Transformer blocks.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Phonetic Mismatch:** If the bridge language lacks specific phonemes present in the target language (e.g., clicks or specific tones), the teacher may provide "noisy" or misleading guidance.
*   **Over-smoothing:** Excessive distillation loss might force the student to ignore unique acoustic characteristics of the target language, leading to a "phonetic accent" in the model's predictions.
*   **Computational Cost:** Training a teacher and then running distillation increases the training GPU-hour requirement compared to simple fine-tuning, though inference costs remain the same.

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

Research Proposal: Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Language Models via
Targeted Capacity Allocation## Title
Beyond Scaling Alone: Targeted Capacity
Allocation for Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Sub-1B Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Small language models (<1B parameters) exhibit a well-documented but
poorly understood phenomenon: diminishing returns past a critical data scale,
where additional tokens yield negligible or even negative performance gains on
held-out benchmarks. This "performance ceiling" is typically attributed to
insufficient model capacity, but recent evidence suggests that capacity is not
uniformly the bottleneck — certain capabilities (e.g., factual recall,
long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,
in-context pattern matching). The research problem is: Can we identify the
precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

Secondary hypothesis: A structured intervention that decouples these two
functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal has three stages:

Stage1: Ceiling CharacterizationTrain a350M-parameter decoder-only transformer
on increasing data scales (50M,100M,250M,500M,1B,2B,5B,10B tokens). At each
checkpoint, measure per-capability saturation curves across five categories:
factual recall, syntactic well-formedness, short-range reasoning (2 hops),
long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which
capability.

Stage2: Bottleneck DiagnosisInsert capacity probes — lightweight linear
classifiers at each layer that predict whether a given capability fires — to
identify the specific (layer, module) pairs where representation collision
occurs. The hypothesis is that mid-to-late FFN layers become the bottleneck for
factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Stage3: Targeted Capacity AllocationIf the diagnosis confirms the hypothesis,
intervene by:

• Retrieval-Augmented Distillation (RAD): Compress the factual knowledge stored
in FFN layers into a small external memory (a frozen key-value store with ~4K
slots). Shrink the model's FFN hidden dimension by25–40% and retrain from
scratch, relying on retrieval for factual queries and freeing FFN capacity
for reasoning.
• Optional control arm: Compare against a naive "bigger FFN" baseline (same
total parameters, no retrieval) to confirm that how capacity is allocated
matters more than how much.

If the diagnosis contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., attention is the bottleneck),
pivot to attention head pruning + reallocation — removing redundant heads to
increase per-head dimensionality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A deduplicated, controlled-quality mix of C4
(natural language), MathPile (math/reasoning), and a synthetic factual QA
dataset (Wiki-QA, ~2M question-answer pairs with provenance). All tokenized with
the same tokenizer to avoid confounds.

• Evaluation (4 benchmarks):
• Factual recall: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA (exact match)
• Short reasoning: BigBench-Hard subset (boolean expressions, causal judgment)
• Long reasoning: GSM8K (grade-school math, multi-step), HotpotQA (multi-hop
retrieval)
• In-context learning: MMLU (5-shot)
• Saturation diagnosis: Custom probe tasks —500 hand-written examples per
capability with controlled difficulty levels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|--------|-----------| | Accuracy (per benchmark) | Primary capability-level
metric | | Saturation threshold (η) | The data scale (in tokens) at which
performance plateaus within1% of final value | | Representation Collapse Score
(RCS) | Average pairwise CKA similarity >0.95 between adjacent data-scale
checkpoints in bottleneck layers — a proxy for when representations stop
differentiating | | Parameter-Utilization Efficiency (PUE) | Per-point
improvement per million train tokens normalized by model size; captures
diminishing returns | | Retrieval Hit Rate (RAD variant only) | Fraction of
queries where the external memory returns the correct factual document |

Primary success signal: RAD variant achieves >10% relative improvement on GSM8K
and HotpotQA over the350M baseline at the same total parameter budget, without
regressing more than2% on NaturalQuestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Standard350M decoder (no intervention) — the ceiling-establishing
baseline2. 350M with increased FFN dimension (+25% FFN, -25% attention heads,
same total params) — tests whether naive capacity reallocation achieves similar
gains3. 350M with vanilla RAG (retrieval + standard model, no capacity
reduction) — tests whether retrieval helps regardless of capacity rebalancing4.
Distilled350M from a7B teacher (knowledge distillation alone) — tests whether
the ceiling is a training limitation vs. architectural5. 550M standard decoder
(more parameters entirely) — the "just scale up" ceiling comparison---

Ablations1. RAD without FFN shrinkage — does retrieval help when FFN capacity is
not freed?

2 RAD with different memory sizes (2K,4K,8K slots) — sensitivity to memory
bottleneck3. RAD applied at different layers (early vs. mid vs. late FFN) —
where is compressed storage most effective?
3 Retrieval-free control — train the shrunken-FFN model without retrieval;
isolates whether the gain comes from the architecture change or the
retrieval5. Ceiling characterization on a different architecture (e.g., a350M
MoE with same total params) — is the ceiling mechanism architecture-specific?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation / Response |

|---|---| | No clear bottleneck emerges (all modules saturate simultaneously) |
The pluralistic-ceiling hypothesis fails. Fallback: test if training recipe (LR
schedule, weight decay) is the real ceiling — ablate optimizer settings. | | RAD
improves reasoning but kills factual recall >2% | Memory size was too small.
Re-run with16K slots or use a learned gating mechanism to route queries. | |
Naive FFN-increase baseline matches or beats RAD | Capacity allocation is not
the bottleneck; the ceiling is truly total-parameter-limited. Concede and report
the negative result as a contribution (important for the community). | | No
ceiling observed (performance continues scaling linearly at10B tokens) | The350M
model was too large for the data scales tested. Scale up to50B tokens or test
a100M model to find the ceiling. | | RAD improves only on seen-document queries
(memorization, not generalization) | Evaluate on held-out timestamps and topics.
If gains vanish, the retrieval store is overfitting to the training set.
Introduce a stricter train/test split on documents. | | CKA-based diagnosis is
inconclusive | Supplement with probing classifiers and leave-one-out accuracy
drops to cross-validate which layers matter for each capability. |

### 1. Title
**Iterative Latent Refinement (ILR): Breaking the Parameter-Depth Ceiling via Recurrent Weight Sharing**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Small Language Models (SLMs) in the 100M to 1.5B parameter range exhibit a "reasoning ceiling." While they can be trained to excel at linguistic fluency and factual retrieval, they consistently fail at complex multi-step reasoning (e.g., GSM8K, Big-Bench Hard) where larger models (70B+) succeed. Current scaling laws suggest that increasing depth is necessary for logic, but increasing depth in SLMs leads to prohibitive inference latency and memory footprints. There is a critical need for a mechanism that increases "effective depth" (computational steps) without increasing "static depth" (parameter count).

### 3. Core Hypothesis
The performance ceiling of small models is not limited by the number of parameters, but by the fixed number of transformation steps applied to a token. By implementing a **Recurrent Transformer Block**—where a hidden state is passed through the same set of weights multiple times—an SLM can simulate the representational power of a much deeper model, effectively decoupling "compute depth" from "parameter count."

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Iterative Latent Refinement (ILR)**, modifies the standard transformer architecture as follows:
1.  **Recurrent Core:** A subset of layers (e.g., layers 4 through 8 in a 12-layer model) is designated as the "Recurrent Core."
2.  **Iterative Processing:** For each token, the hidden state enters the core and is processed $N$ times (where $N$ is a hyperparameter or dynamically determined) before moving to the final output layers.
3.  **Cross-Iteration Consistency:** To prevent latent state drift, we apply:
    *   **Weight-Tying:** The weights of the recurrent core are shared across all $N$ iterations.
    *   **Recurrent LayerNorm:** A specialized normalization step to stabilize the variance of the hidden state across iterations.
    *   **Iteration Embedding:** A small learnable vector added to the hidden state to inform the model which iteration ($1 \dots N$) it is currently performing.
4.  **Training Objective:** The model is trained using a "Multi-Exit" loss, where the model is encouraged to produce the correct token prediction at any iteration $i \in [1, N]$, though the final loss is weighted toward the $N$-th iteration.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Primary Benchmark:** **GSM8K** (Grade School Math) and **MATH**, to test logical depth.
*   **Secondary Benchmark:** **Big-Bench Hard (BBH)**, specifically the "Reasoning about Colored Objects" and "Logical Deduction" tasks.
*   **Pre-training Corpus:** A 100B token subset of **FineWeb-Edu** to ensure the model has high-quality reasoning signals.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Accuracy (Pass@1):** Performance on reasoning tasks.
*   **Compute-Efficiency Ratio (CER):** Accuracy divided by the number of unique parameters.
*   **Inference Latency vs. Accuracy:** A Pareto curve comparing ILR models against standard models with equivalent FLOPs.
*   **Stability Score:** Variance of the hidden state across iterations (to measure latent collapse).

### 7. Baselines
1.  **Standard Transformer:** A vanilla Llama-style model with the same number of parameters (e.g., 1.1B parameters, 12 layers).
2.  **Deep-Narrow Baseline:** A model with the same *total* FLOPs as the ILR model but achieved through unique layers (e.g., a 48-layer model with smaller hidden dimension).
3.  **MobileLLM:** A state-of-the-art small model baseline utilizing weight sharing but without iterative refinement logic.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Iteration Count ($N$):** Testing $N=1$ (baseline) vs. $N=2, 4, 8$.
*   **Weight Sharing vs. Unique Weights:** Comparing the ILR core against a "Deep" model of the same depth but with unique parameters to isolate the benefit of recurrence.
*   **Dynamic vs. Static $N$:** Testing if a "halt signal" (Adaptive Computation Time) outperforms a fixed number of iterations.
*   **Iteration Embeddings:** Evaluating performance with and without the iteration-specific learnable vectors.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Vanishing/Exploding Gradients:** Repeated application of the same weights may lead to numerical instability. *Mitigation:* Use of ReZero or strict LayerNorm scaling.
*   **Latent State Stagnation:** The model may learn a "null transformation" where iterations 2 through $N$ do not change the hidden state. *Mitigation:* Implement a "Residual Difference" penalty to ensure each iteration adds information.
*   **Inference Overhead:** While parameter-efficient, $N$ iterations still cost $N \times$ FLOPs. The feasibility depends on whether weight-sharing provides better generalization than simply using a larger, non-recurrent model of the same FLOP count.

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis

observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode
or bullet points) before execution, then follows it linearly, but does not
re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

• Plan: Writes an explicit, numbered plan with preconditions and expected
postconditions for each step.
• Trace: After each observation, appends a structured trace entry: [Step N]
expected=<...> observed=<...> match=<yes|no>.
• Verify: Before the next step, runs a consistency check. If match=no, the
agent must decide: (a) proceed (the mismatch is benign), (b) re-plan from
this state, or (c) request clarification.

• Clean: Standard trajectory, no distractors.
• Weak distractors: One irrelevant observation per task, semantically related
to the domain but logically unnecessary (e.g., a flight search returns "Did
you know? Economy seats have30-inch pitch." between steps).
• Strong distractors: Two to three irrelevant observations, written to
plausibly contradict an intermediate expectation without actually
invalidating the correct path (e.g., a weather lookup returns "Rain expected"
when the correct reasoning only needs temperature).

Distractors are inserted at fixed positions (after step1, after step2) to ensure
controlled comparison.

compositional reasoning dataset with500 tasks spanning three domains:

citations that also use
dataset Y"

Tokyo, convert to UTC, find
a meeting slot that works
for a New York participant"

distractor surface form variationWe also evaluate on AgentQA (a subset of200

correct action/observation is selected given the history | Yes | | Final answer
accuracy | Exact-match (or programmatic equivalence) of the final output | Yes |

from the optimal plan (measured by trace alignment) | Secondary | | Recovery
rate | Fraction of distractor episodes where the agent corrects itself before
the final step | Secondary | | Token cost overhead | Total input + output tokens
relative to Direct-ReAct | Efficiency |

minimal agent; lower bound | | Plan-then-Execute | Pre-plan, no mid-trajectory
verification | Isolates the value of verification vs planning | | ReAct +

verbalizes feedback after failure | Tests whether post-hoc reflection recovers
from distractors | | GPT-4o / Claude3.5 Sonnet (zero-shot) | No ReAct, just

**1. Title**
RE-PLAN: Recursive Error-Correction via Latent Planning and Simulation in Multi-Step Agentic Tasks.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current Large Language Model (LLM) agents often suffer from "cascading failures" in long-horizon reasoning tasks. When an agent makes an initial sub-optimal decision or encounters an unexpected environment state, it tends to rationalize the error in its subsequent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rather than correcting it. This is primarily due to the linear nature of standard autoregressive generation. While frameworks like ReAct (Reason + Act) allow for environment feedback, they lack a "look-ahead" mechanism to simulate the potential consequences of an action before committing to it, leading to irreversible state changes in complex environments.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating a "Simulation-then-Execution" loop—where the agent generates multiple latent trajectories (simulations), evaluates them using an internal critic, and selects the path with the highest predicted success probability—will significantly improve performance on multi-step reasoning benchmarks compared to reactive (ReAct) or purely linear (CoT) baselines.

**4. Method**
The RE-PLAN framework consists of three distinct modules:
*   **Proposer (P):** Given a goal and current state $S_t$, the Proposer generates $K$ candidate action sequences $\{A_1, A_2, ... A_K\}$ for the next $N$ steps.
*   **Simulator (S):** For each candidate sequence, the Simulator (an LLM prompted to act as a world model) predicts the resulting state $S_{t+N}$ and the likely environment feedback.
*   **Critic (C):** A reward-modeling prompt evaluates the simulated states $S_{t+N}$ against the global goal, assigning a score.
*   **Execution:** The agent selects the highest-scored sequence, executes the first action in the real environment, and then triggers a recursive check: if the actual environment feedback deviates significantly from the simulated prediction, the agent flushes the current plan and triggers a re-simulation.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
The proposal will utilize **ALFWorld**, a synthetic environment that requires agents to solve multi-step household tasks (e.g., "put a clean sponge in the cabinet") using text-based interactions. ALFWorld is ideal because it requires both high-level planning and low-level state tracking, and provides a deterministic ground truth for success.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Success Rate (SR):** The percentage of tasks completed within the maximum step limit (50 steps).
*   **Goal Progress (GP):** For failed tasks, the percentage of sub-goals completed.
*   **Path Efficiency Ratio:** The ratio of the length of the optimal path (determined by an oracle) to the length of the agent’s actual path.
*   **Inference Cost:** Measured in total tokens per successful task completion to evaluate the trade-off between reasoning depth and compute.

**7. Baselines**
*   **ReAct:** The standard Reason + Act paradigm (Yao et al., 2022).
*   **Reflexion:** An agent that performs linguistic self-reflection after a task failure to improve the next trial (Shinn et al., 2023).
*   **CoT-Prompting:** A zero-shot or few-shot Chain-of-Thought baseline without environment interaction.

**8. Ablations**
*   **No-Simulation:** The Proposer generates only one path (K=1) and executes it without Critic evaluation.
*   **No-Correction:** The agent follows the simulated plan even if the real environment feedback contradicts the simulation.
*   **Random Critic:** Instead of an LLM-based Critic, a random sequence is selected from the $K$ candidates to test the necessity of the evaluation step.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Simulation Drift:** The LLM acting as the "Simulator" may provide inaccurate predictions of environment transitions, leading the agent to optimize for a "hallucinated" state.
*   **Inference Latency:** Generating $K$ trajectories and evaluating them significantly increases the time and cost per action.
*   **State-Space Explosion:** In very complex environments, $K$ simulations may not be enough to find a viable path, leading to performance plateaus.
*   **Feasibility:** Using high-throughput APIs (like GPT-4o-mini or Llama-3-70B) is necessary to keep the computational cost manageable while maintaining the reasoning quality required for the Simulator/Critic roles.

SAM-Quant: Sensitivity-Aware Mixed-Precision Quantization for Resource-Constrained Edge LLMs.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson, mobile SoCs, Raspberry Pi) is constrained by limited VRAM and memory bandwidth. While 4-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) techniques like GPTQ or AWQ significantly reduce footprint, they often lead to substantial "accuracy collapse" in smaller models (3B–8B parameters) which are the primary candidates for edge deployment. Current methods typically apply uniform bit-widths across all layers, failing to account for the fact that certain "bottleneck" layers or attention heads are significantly more sensitive to precision loss than others.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
A non-uniform, mixed-precision allocation—where <10% of layers identified through Hessian-based sensitivity analysis are retained in 8-bit while the remainder are compressed to 3-bit or 4-bit—will yield a Pareto-superior trade-off between model perplexity and inference latency compared to uniform 4-bit quantization.

**4. Method**
The proposed method, SAM-Quant, consists of three stages:
1.  **Sensitivity Profiling:** For a given model (e.g., Llama-3-8B), compute the Fisher Information Matrix or the trace of the Hessian for each layer using a small calibration set (e.g., 128 samples from Pile/C4).
2.  **Budget-Constrained Optimization:** Formulate an optimization problem where the objective is to minimize the total reconstruction error $\sum ||W x - \hat{W} x||^2$ subject to a hard memory constraint (e.g., total model size < 5.5 GB).
3.  **Mixed-Precision Mapping:** Assign bit-widths (2, 3, 4, or 8-bit) to layers based on the sensitivity ranking. Highly sensitive layers (often the first and last blocks) receive higher precision.
4.  **Kernel Implementation:** Use a specialized CUDA/OpenCL kernel that supports mixed-precision dequantization on-the-fly, ensuring that the overhead of switching bit-widths does not negate the speed gains from quantization.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Calibration:** 128 segments of 2048 tokens from the **C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus)**.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **Language Modeling:** WikiText-2 and PTB (Perplexity).
    *   **Downstream Tasks:** MMLU (General knowledge), GSM8K (Reasoning), and HumanEval (Coding).
    *   **Hardware Target:** NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (simulated or physical) and MacBook M2 (using MLX).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Accuracy:** Zero-shot accuracy on MMLU and GSM8K.
*   **Compression:** Total model size in Gigabytes (GB).
*   **Efficiency:** Tokens per second (TPS) and Time-to-First-Token (TTFT).
*   **Quality:** Perplexity (PPL) on WikiText-2.

**7. Baselines**
*   **FP16:** The uncompressed reference model.
*   **RTN (Round-to-Nearest):** Standard 4-bit uniform quantization.
*   **GPTQ:** Optimal Brain Quantization-based 4-bit uniform.
*   **AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization):** Current state-of-the-art for uniform 4-bit weight-only quantization.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Layer Selection Strategy:** Compare SAM-Quant sensitivity ranking against random layer selection and uniform layer selection.
*   **Calibration Size:** Test the impact of using 32, 64, 128, and 256 calibration samples on final accuracy.
*   **Bit-width Granularity:** Compare per-channel vs. per-group quantization within the mixed-precision framework.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Kernel Overhead:** The primary risk is that the logic required to handle different bit-widths in a single forward pass may introduce branching kernels that slow down inference, potentially making a 4-bit uniform model faster despite SAM-Quant being more accurate.
*   **Calibration Drift:** The sensitivity of layers might be task-specific; a model optimized for C4 might underperform on specialized medical or legal datasets.
*   **Hardware Support:** Not all edge accelerators support sub-byte arithmetic efficiently (e.g., 3-bit), which may require packing/unpacking overhead in software.

Research Proposal: Schema-Aware Decomposition for Complex Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases## Title
Schema-Aware Decomposition: Robust Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases via Progressive Pruning and Incremental Construction

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary evaluation on BIRD-SQL (2024), specifically its
large-scale subset (databases with ≥30 tables: ~15–20 databases, ~1,500
questions). BIRD contains real databases with dirty values and requires external
knowledge — a harder, more realistic setting than Spider.

For controlled analysis, also evaluate on Spider-Syn (schema synonym variant,
~700 questions) and Spider-Realistic (~500 questions with paraphrased
questions), which stress schema linking.

If results are strong, test a synthetic Spider-XL dataset constructed by
concatenating3–4 Spider databases into a single schema (~60 tables,200+ columns)
with200 cross-database questions written by hand.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Why |

|---|---|---| | Execution Accuracy (ExA) | % of predicted SQL queries whose
execution output matches the gold output | Primary metric; forgiving of
syntactic alternatives | | Exact Set Match (ESM) | % of predicted SQL that
exactly matches gold AST (canonicalized) | Measures structural correctness | |
Schema Recall (SR) | % of gold-referenced tables/columns present in the pruned
schema | Stage1 diagnostic | | Decomposition Fidelity | % of sub-queries that
correctly map to gold sub-expressions (manual eval on200 random samples) |
Stage2 diagnostic | | LLM calls per query | Average number of API calls per
question | Cost/latency diagnostic | | Success@1 vs Success@5 | Accuracy without
and with self-consistency (5 samples) | Robustness check |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Method | Category | Why included |

|---|---|---| | Flat prompt (full schema) | Baseline | Upper-bound approximation
(fails when schema exceeds context) | | Flat prompt (truncated schema, first N
tables) | Baseline | Current naive approach | | DAIL-SQL (few-shot prompt +
schema filtering) | Strong few-shot | State-of-the-art on Spider with GPT-4 | |
DIN-SQL (task decomposition via LLM) | Decomposition | Direct competitor — tests
whether our structured decomposition beats its unstructured approach | | MAC-SQL
(multi-agent collaboration) | Multi-agent | Tests whether explicit decomposition
beats agentic coordination | | CHASE-SQL (code generation + execution) |
Execution-feedback | Tests whether our incremental verifier beats post-hoc
execution feedback |

All baselines evaluated with the same backbone LLM (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o) on
the same hardware/API version.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Pruning ablation: Compare structure-aware + semantic vs.
semantic-only vs. embedding-only (Stage1 variants).

2 Decomposition ablation: Remove Stage2 entirely; feed pruned schema directly
to Stage3.
3 Verification ablation: Remove local verifier (no sub-query execution check);
only final assembly check.

### 1. Title
**CAR-SQL: Constraint-Anchored Reasoning for Robust Text-to-SQL Generation in Large-Scale Databases**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved high performance on Text-to-SQL benchmarks like Spider, they often fail in real-world scenarios characterized by massive schemas (hundreds of tables) and complex relational constraints. Current models frequently suffer from "Schema Hallucination"—referencing columns that do not exist or joining tables on incompatible keys—and "Constraint Neglect," where they ignore foreign key (FK) relationships essential for data integrity. There is a need for a methodology that forces the model to reason about the database’s relational integrity *before* generating the final query.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Incorporating an explicit "Relational Integrity Verification" (RIV) step—where the model must map natural language entities to specific Primary Key-Foreign Key (PK-FK) paths before drafting the SELECT and WHERE clauses—will significantly reduce execution errors in multi-join queries compared to standard chain-of-thought or zero-shot prompting.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Constraint-Anchored Reasoning (CAR)**, follows a three-stage pipeline:

1.  **Schema Pruning & Constraint Extraction:** Given a natural language question (NLQ) and a full schema (DDL), the model first identifies a sub-schema of potentially relevant tables. For these tables, it extracts all PK-FK relationships and "CHECK" constraints.
2.  **Constraint Path Mapping (The Core Innovation):** The model is prompted to generate a "Relational Path" in a structured format (e.g., `TableA.ID -> TableB.A_ID`). It must justify why this path is necessary to answer the NLQ. This forces the model to anchor its logic in the database's physical constraints.
3.  **Constraint-Anchored Generation:** The model generates the final SQL query, using the Relational Path from Stage 2 as a mandatory blueprint. If the SQL uses a join not specified in the path, a self-correction module triggers a re-generation.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Primary Benchmark:** **BIRD (Big Bench for Large-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)**. BIRD is chosen over Spider because it contains larger databases (up to 100GB), more complex schemas, and requires higher "database-savvy" reasoning.
*   **Subset:** Focus on the "Challenging" and "External Knowledge" categories within BIRD, where relational mapping is most critical.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Execution Accuracy (EX):** The percentage of predicted queries that return the same result set as the gold query.
*   **Valid Efficiency Score (VES):** Measures the execution efficiency of the generated SQL, rewarding queries that utilize indexes and correct join orders.
*   **Schema Linkage Precision/Recall:** A manual or model-based audit of whether the correct PK-FK pairs were identified in Stage 2.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Zero-shot/Few-shot GPT-4o:** Standard prompting without explicit constraint reasoning.
*   **DIN-SQL (Decomposed In-Context Learning):** The current state-of-the-art approach that uses task decomposition (classification, SQL generation, self-correction).
*   **DAIL-SQL:** A benchmark baseline that optimizes prompt selection and organization for Text-to-SQL.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No-Constraint Mapping:** Remove Stage 2 and provide the pruned schema directly to the generator.
*   **Implicit vs. Explicit Constraints:** Compare providing the model with a list of FKs versus forcing it to write out the "Relational Path" before the SQL.
*   **Static vs. Dynamic Pruning:** Compare using the full DDL versus the pruned sub-schema from Stage 1.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Inference Latency:** The multi-stage pipeline (Pruning -> Mapping -> Generation) increases token usage and wall-clock time, which may be impractical for real-time applications.
*   **Schema Noise:** In poorly designed legacy databases where FK constraints are not explicitly defined in the DDL, the "Constraint Mapping" stage may fail to find valid paths.
*   **Over-reliance on PK-FK:** The model might struggle with "Ad-hoc Joins" (joins on columns that are not formally linked in the schema) if it becomes too rigid in its constraint-anchoring.

Research Proposal: Disentangling Knowledge from Reasoning in LLMs via Controlled
Representation Intervention## Title
Disentangling Knowledge and Reasoning
Pathways in LLMs: A Representation-Intervention Framework for Capability
Decoupling

Problem
Large Language Models integrate multiple capabilities — factual
knowledge, logical reasoning, instruction following, and stylistic control —
into a single monolithic forward pass. This entanglement creates three concrete
problems:

1 Uninterpretability: When a model answers incorrectly, we cannot attribute the
failure to missing knowledge vs. faulty reasoning.
2 Brittle editing: Model editing (e.g., MEMIT, ROME) modifies factual knowledge
but can degrade downstream reasoning performance, suggesting the two share
overlapping representations.
3 Incapability of compositional control: We cannot independently upgrade a
model's reasoning ability without affecting its knowledge base, or vice

**1. Title**
DECOUPLE-LOGIC: Benchmarking and Isolating Factual Knowledge from Logical Reasoning via Counterfactual Intervention.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current Large Language Models (LLMs) conflate two distinct capabilities: **internalized factual knowledge** (memorized data) and **logical reasoning** (the ability to manipulate rules). This coupling leads to "reasoning by memorization," where a model appears to solve a complex problem only because it has seen the specific instance or a near-identical pattern in its training set.

This lack of decoupling presents a significant bottleneck for:
*   **Generalization:** Models fail when encountering novel scenarios that contradict their training data.
*   **Reliability:** Hallucinations often occur when a model’s "reasoning" is overridden by a strong, but incorrect, factual prior.
*   **Evaluation:** Current benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MMLU) are contaminated, making it impossible to tell if a model is "thinking" or "retrieving."

**3. Core Hypothesis**
The reasoning performance of an LLM is inversely correlated with the "factual distance" of the prompt from its training distribution. By applying counterfactual interventions to logical premises, we can quantify the degree of coupling and isolate a "Pure Reasoning Score" (PRS) that is independent of world knowledge.

**4. Method**
The proposed method involves a three-stage intervention pipeline:
1.  **Fact-Logic Mapping:** Deconstruct standard logical problems (syllogisms, mathematical word problems, or programming logic) into their structural components (the "logic graph") and their semantic components (the "entities").
2.  **Counterfactual Swapping:** Systematically replace semantic entities with:
    *   *Category A (Factual):* The original, true-to-world premises.
    *   *Category B (Counterfactual):* Premises that are logically valid but factually false (e.g., "The sun is made of ice; ice is hot; therefore the sun is hot").
    *   *Category C (Abstract):* Premises using nonsense or symbolic tokens (e.g., "Gorp is a Blerp; Blerps are Zazz; therefore Gorp is Zazz").
3.  **Inference & Extraction:** Run the model on all categories. A "Decoupled" model should maintain identical accuracy across all three, while a "Coupled" model will show high performance on A and significant degradation on B and C.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
**The LogicSwap Benchmark:**
*   **Source:** 2,000 samples derived from pruned subsets of Big-Bench (Logical Deduction) and GSM8K.
*   **Structure:** Each sample is provided in three variants: *Standard*, *Counterfactual*, and *Abstract*.
*   **Validation:** All counterfactual variants must be manually verified to ensure that the logical validity of the conclusion remains unchanged despite the factual falsity of the premises.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Decoupling Delta ($\Delta D$):** The percentage drop in accuracy between Factual and Counterfactual prompts. $\Delta D = (Acc_{Factual} - Acc_{Counterfactual}) / Acc_{Factual}$.
*   **Pure Reasoning Score (PRS):** The model’s accuracy on the Abstract variant, representing the baseline for content-independent logic.
*   **Reasoning Consistency (RC):** The frequency with which the model provides the same logical derivation steps across all three variants, regardless of the correctness of the final answer.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Zero-Shot CoT:** Standard Chain-of-Thought prompting on base models (e.g., Llama-3-70B, GPT-4o).
*   **Few-Shot In-Context Learning (ICL):** Providing 3-5 examples of counterfactual reasoning to see if the model can be "primed" to decouple.
*   **Instruction-Tuned Baselines:** Models specifically tuned for logic (e.g., Orca-2 or specialized math models).

**8. Ablations**
*   **Entity Familiarity:** Vary the counterfactuals from "slightly false" (The moon is made of silver) to "highly dissonant" (Fire is freezing) to measure if the degree of factual violation affects the reasoning breakdown.
*   **Prompt Formatting:** Test if different delimiters (e.g., "Assume for the sake of argument...") reduce the coupling effect.
*   **Model Size:** Compare 7B, 13B, and 70B+ parameter models to determine if larger models exhibit more or less coupling.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Safety Filter Interference:** Models may refuse to process counterfactuals if they trigger "misinformation" or "helpfulness" guardrails (e.g., refusing to say "The sun is cold").
*   **Semantic Drift:** In the Abstract category, models may lose the "semantic scaffolding" required to understand the prompt structure, leading to a baseline collapse that isn't related to logic.
*   **Feasibility:** Creating 2,000 high-quality counterfactuals requires rigorous quality control to ensure that the logic is not inadvertently broken during the swap (e.g., swapping a noun for a verb). This will be mitigated by using a template-based generation approach followed by a subset of human verification.

Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs

Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel

as the reference.

### 1. Title
**Contrastive Knowledge-Augmented Decoding (CKAD): Improving Factual Consistency via Logit-Space Distribution Shifting**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit "factual inconsistency," where generated content contradicts either external reality or the model’s own internal knowledge base. A primary driver of this is the "fluency-factuality tradeoff": the model’s training objective (next-token prediction) prioritizes high-probability linguistic sequences over grounding. Current solutions like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often fail when the model’s internal prior (parametric memory) is stronger than the provided context, leading the model to ignore factual evidence in favor of common hallucinations.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Factual consistency can be significantly improved by isolating the "hallucination signal." By calculating the difference in log-probabilities between a context-aware model and a context-blind model during decoding, we can amplify tokens supported by evidence and suppress tokens generated purely from biased parametric priors.

### 4. Method
The proposed method, **Contrastive Knowledge-Augmented Decoding (CKAD)**, operates during the inference phase without requiring model retraining:

1.  **Dual-Stream Logit Generation:** For every token $t$, compute two sets of logits:
    *   $L_{grounded}$: Logits produced by the model provided with a factual context (e.g., a retrieved snippet).
    *   $L_{prior}$: Logits produced by the model without the factual context (or with a generic prompt).
2.  **Contrastive Re-weighting:** Calculate the adjusted logit $L'_{t}$ as:
    $L'_{t} = L_{grounded} + \alpha \cdot (L_{grounded} - L_{prior})$
    where $\alpha$ is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of the factual grounding.
3.  **Adaptive Thresholding:** To prevent linguistic incoherence, apply the contrastive shift only to tokens where the entropy of $L_{grounded}$ is high, suggesting the model is uncertain and prone to hallucination.
4.  **Decoding:** Sample the next token from the softmax of $L'_{t}$.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
The evaluation will utilize the **HaluEval** dataset and the **FactScore** framework.
*   **HaluEval:** Specifically the "Summarization" and "Question Answering" subsets, which contain paired factual and hallucinated samples.
*   **FactScore:** A benchmark that breaks down long-form generations into individual atomic facts and verifies them against Wikipedia.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **FactScore (Primary):** Percentage of generated atomic facts supported by a knowledge source.
*   **Knowledge F1:** Measure of overlap between the generated facts and the ground-truth reference context.
*   **MAUVE / Perplexity:** To ensure that the contrastive decoding does not degrade the linguistic fluency or "naturalness" of the text.
*   **Hallucination Rate:** Percentage of model outputs that contradict the provided context in HaluEval.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard RAG:** Greedy decoding using the retrieved context in the prompt.
*   **Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting:** Asking the model to "think step-by-step" before asserting a fact.
*   **Self-Correction (Self-CheckGPT):** A post-hoc method where the model is asked to review its own output for errors.
*   **Decoding by Contrast (Dola):** A baseline that contrasts different layers of the model rather than context-aware/context-blind streams.

### 8. Ablations
*   **$\alpha$ Sensitivity:** Testing values of $\alpha$ from 0.1 to 2.0 to find the "sweet spot" between factuality and fluency.
*   **Context Quality:** Replacing the factual context with "garbage" or "distractor" text to see if CKAD correctly identifies when to rely on the prior.
*   **Logit vs. Probability Space:** Comparing the contrastive shift in the logit space versus the raw probability space.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Linguistic Degradation:** Excessive $\alpha$ values may lead to repetitive or ungrammatical text as the model ignores the natural language flow in favor of factual keywords.
*   **Inference Latency:** Generating two sets of logits per token doubles the computational cost. This can be mitigated by using a smaller "draft" model for the $L_{prior}$ stream.
*   **Context Dependency:** If the retrieved context is itself incorrect, CKAD will amplify the error more aggressively than standard RAG. This requires a high-precision retrieval component.

Code LLM Reasoning## Title

Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

correct code without showing the failure context.

training itself?).

that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.
